**Why the pier logger reads warmer than the offshore buoy**

A few of you have now emailed asking why my pier logger runs warmer than the offshore buoy, and one of you suggested, politely, that the thing might be broken. It isn't. Here's the short version so we can put the guessing to rest.

The October mean was 15.9 °C at the pier logger against 14.1 °C at the buoy — about a 1.8 °C gap. By winter that gap shrinks to roughly 0.4 °C.

That pattern is what you'd expect from where the two instruments actually sit. The logger is strapped to a piling at 3 m depth, about 150 m from shore, in sheltered bay water. The buoy is ~25 km offshore with its sensor just under the surface over deep water. Shallow nearshore water warms in the sun, and the bay is sheltered from the upwelling that keeps the offshore water cold. One reader sent me a screenshot with both records overlaid, which was genuinely helpful: the gap tracks sunny afternoons almost exactly. That's oceanography, not a drifting sensor.

On the instrument itself: it logs every 10 minutes, I pull and download it every six weeks, and I swap the battery once a year. The calibration check is two-point — an ice bath and a room-temperature bath — run against a lab reference thermometer. Last check was September 2026: offset +0.12 °C, well inside spec. In August I hauled it up with a barnacle colony and a decorator crab living on the housing, scraped it clean, and the readings didn't change.

The real point is that the buoy and the logger answer different questions. The buoy tells you about offshore, open-water conditions. Mine tells you what the water is doing at the pier. If you're diving the breakwater, mine is the more relevant number.

If you want to poke at the data yourself, email me and I'll send the raw CSV.

— [Name], [Field Station]
